topics.definition: A linked list is a linear data structure where elements (nodes) are connected using pointers.
tips: Nodes are not stored in contiguous memory.

topics.definition: A node contains data and a pointer to the next node.
topics.syntax: struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; };
tips: The last node points to NULL in a singly linked list.

topics.definition: Insertion adds a new node at the beginning, end or a specific position.
Deletion removes a node from the linked list.
tips: Free deleted node memory in C.

topics.definition: Traversal visits every node from head to NULL.
Each node points to the next node only.
Each node has pointers to both previous and next nodes.
tips: Uses more memory than singly linked lists.

topics.definition: The last node points back to the first node.
Linked lists allow dynamic memory allocation but have slower random access.
Common programs include insertion, deletion, reversal, searching and counting nodes.
tips: Frequently asked in exams and interviews.
